drhp.business: GOCL Corporation, established in 1961 as Indian Detonators Limited and formerly Gulf Oil Corporation, divested IDL Explosives Limited and discontinued its Energetics operations, and is now engaged in Electronics Manufacturing Services and Realty. GOCL-EMS positions itself as a niche ODM solutions provider offering product design and engineering, prototyping, PCB assembly, box-build integration, testing and fulfilment to OEMs, while the realty business is monetising land at Hyderabad and the Ecopolis project at Bengaluru. The company is transitioning into thermal power generation through a Scheme of Merger of Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited (HNPCL), subject to requisite approvals.
drhp.end_markets: Electric mobility (EV)|Aerospace and defence|Industrial electronics|Internet of Things (IoT)|Consumer electronics|Telecommunications|Automotive|Domestic India only (6 states; no exports this year)
drhp.expansion: During FY 2025-26 GOCL commissioned a new 3-acre EMS manufacturing facility at Gummadidala, near Hyderabad, relocating the EMS operations there; it is fully operational after receiving its factory licence and has automated SMT lines, MES, 3D SPI and 3D AOI to take on large OEM programmes. The main expansion move is inorganic: a Scheme of Merger of Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited, approved by the Board on December 15, 2025 and expected to complete shortly subject to statutory and regulatory approvals, would bring in an operational 1,040 MW (2x520 MW) coal-based plant near Visakhapatnam, commissioned around 2016. HNPCL has a planned 600 MW brownfield expansion, with available land, water infrastructure and rail connectivity, and long-term options for FGD retrofits and ammonia/hydrogen pilot co-firing. No timeline is given for the brownfield expansion. On the realty side the company is monetising rather than building: sale of land at Kukatpally, Hyderabad and sale of the entire Ecopolis project at Bengaluru.

demand_drivers.title: Mdna (RHP)
demand_drivers.body:
- HNPCL's region near Visakhapatnam is emerging as a hub for industrial development and data centre investment (Google, Meta and HCL Tech cited), which management expects to drive sustained growth in electricity demand.
- Rising peak demand and policy tailwinds have renewed thermal planning; thermal capacity requirement estimated at approximately 3,07,000 MW by 2034-35, with ~70-80 GW of coal-based capacity being considered for 2028-2032.
- Government has ensured adequate coal supply to thermal plants for peak-hour generation, supporting higher plant utilisation; the company initiated the HNPCL merger to exploit this.
- HNPCL is expected to benefit from recovery in power demand across the Southern Region; management says the merger will enhance operational scale and strengthen the resilience of cash flows, though some tariff/regulatory issues need active management.
- India's EMS industry is shifting from contract manufacturing to ODM, supported by PLI, the expanded Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme and the India Semiconductor Mission.
- EMS headwind: rising cost of doing business from wages, labour inflation, logistics and raw materials.
- Real-estate demand supported by government road, rail and logistics infrastructure and growth in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.

capex_expansion.title: Expansion (RHP)
capex_expansion.body: During FY 2025-26 GOCL commissioned a new 3-acre EMS manufacturing facility at Gummadidala, near Hyderabad, relocating the EMS operations there; it is fully operational after receiving its factory licence and has automated SMT lines, MES, 3D SPI and 3D AOI to take on large OEM programmes. The main expansion move is inorganic: a Scheme of Merger of Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited, approved by the Board on December 15, 2025 and expected to complete shortly subject to statutory and regulatory approvals, would bring in an operational 1,040 MW (2x520 MW) coal-based plant near Visakhapatnam, commissioned around 2016. HNPCL has a planned 600 MW brownfield expansion, with available land, water infrastructure and rail connectivity, and long-term options for FGD retrofits and ammonia/hydrogen pilot co-firing. No timeline is given for the brownfield expansion. On the realty side the company is monetising rather than building: sale of land at Kukatpally, Hyderabad and sale of the entire Ecopolis project at Bengaluru.

moat.title: Strengths (RHP)
moat.body:
- customer lock-in: the thermal asset GOCL is merging in sells under long-term contracts — evidence: HNPCL's 1,040 MW (2x520 MW) coal plant near Visakhapatnam is 'supported by long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and coal supply agreements' — against it: HNPCL is not yet part of GOCL; the Scheme of Merger is 'subject to requisite approvals'
- resource: a coastal thermal site with infrastructure for further capacity — evidence: HNPCL's site has grid evacuation infrastructure, port access, water infrastructure, available land and a residual plant life of over 20 years, supporting a planned 600 MW brownfield expansion [planned] — against it: the merger is still subject to requisite approvals and the rail corridor is still under construction

risks.title: Risks (RHP)
risks.body:
- Land-sale proceeds from about 157.21 acres at Hyderabad have been temporarily deployed in inter-corporate loans; the company flags the risk of delays or shortfalls in loan recoveries hurting cash flows, asset quality and capital deployment.
- The main operating segment (Energetics and Explosives) has been discontinued and the major revenue in FY 2025-26 came from sale of land, so the company says current key financials are not comparable with previous years.
- The power-sector entry depends on the Scheme of Merger by Absorption of HNPCL, which is subject to requisite approvals.
- Environmental and operational risks may bring regulatory penalties, disruptions and higher costs; delays in obtaining approvals and licences may affect project timelines and business expansion.
- The company may face intense competition from domestic and international players; mitigation is differentiated offerings and niche product development in EMS.
- Wages, labour inflation, logistics and raw-material costs are named as a major obstacle for EMS companies; geopolitical frictions and trade restrictions also disrupt freight routes for industrial parts.
- Sub-par rainfall and El Nino effects cause cooling-water shortages at thermal plants while raising electricity demand, relevant to the planned thermal power business.
- Prolonged litigation, including tax and regulatory disputes, may lead to penalties and management distraction; greater technology integration raises exposure to cybersecurity threats and IT failures.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Board identified Energy and Electronics as the sectors for the company's next phase, after largely completing the portfolio realignment (divestment of IDL Explosives, exit from detonators/explosives).
- Enter thermal power inorganically rather than greenfield: the Board rejected new thermal builds (heavy capex, 6-10 years to commission, coal-linkage and clearance delays) and chose to acquire the operational 1,040 MW HNPCL plant through a Scheme of Merger, approved by the Board on December 15, 2025.
- Deploy the financial surplus from exiting the legacy business and monetising factory land into a sustainable, scalable business.
- Monetise real-estate assets: land at Kukatpally, Hyderabad and early monetisation of the Bengaluru Ecopolis project by sale of the entire project.
- Reposition GOCL-EMS as a niche ODM solutions provider: build Design for Manufacturability capabilities, expand engineering support, increase local value addition, develop indigenous product designs and grow the share of ODM-led business.
- Expand EMS into high-growth sectors: industrial electronics, defence, IoT, automotive and e-mobility; improve efficiency and automation for margin expansion.
